Anticipating On-Target Drug Effects with HPO Gene-Phenotype Data

Source: vignettes/articles/hpo_target_phenotypes.Rmd
hpo_target_phenotypes.Rmd

Introduction

People who carry rare loss-of-function variants in a gene are a natural experiment: they show what happens when the protein that gene encodes stops working for a lifetime. When that protein is also a drug target, their phenotypes are a preview of what the drug might do. Drug discovery teams use this idea to support targets and to anticipate on-target adverse effects before clinical data exist.

The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) annotates genes with the clinical features of the Mendelian diseases they cause. dbparser reads the HPO gene-phenotype associations distributed by Harmonizome with parseHPO(). It then links them to DrugBank targets by gene symbol with merge_drugbank_hpo().

This vignette asks one question for three drugs:

Do the Mendelian phenotypes of a drug’s target genes agree with what we already know about the drug’s therapeutic and adverse effects?

The three drugs act through different mechanisms:

Drug Main target Use
Bivalirudin Thrombin (F2) Anticoagulant during coronary interventions
Leuprolide GnRH receptor (GNRHR) Androgen deprivation, endometriosis
Calcitriol Vitamin D receptor (VDR) Hypocalcaemia, renal bone disease

Prerequisites 

library(dbparser)
library(dplyr)
library(canvasXpress)

1. Load the data

1.1 HPO gene-phenotype associations

The package ships a subset of the Harmonizome HPO file with every association for seven genes. To analyse all genes, download gene_attribute_edges.txt.gz from Harmonizome and pass its path to parseHPO(); gzip-compressed files are read directly.

hpo_db <- parseHPO(
  system.file("extdata", "hpo_gene_attribute_edges.txt", package = "dbparser"),
  db_version = "Harmonizome 2015")

hpo_db$genes
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   gene_symbol entrez_id n_phenotypes
#>   <chr>       <chr>            <int>
#> 1 F2          2147                71
#> 2 GNRH1       2796                24
#> 3 GNRHR       2798                30
#> 4 KCNQ2       3785                69
#> 5 MPO         4353                 7
#> 6 SCN1A       6323               101
#> 7 VDR         7421               183

search_phenotypes() and get_genes_for_phenotype() help explore the phenotypes:

search_phenotypes(hpo_db, "bleeding")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   hpo_id     phenotype_name          n_genes genes
#>   <chr>      <chr>                     <int> <chr>
#> 1 HP:0000225 gingival bleeding             1 F2   
#> 2 HP:0001892 abnormal bleeding             1 F2   
#> 3 HP:0003010 prolonged bleeding time       1 F2
get_genes_for_phenotype(hpo_db, "hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism", exact = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   gene_symbol entrez_id hpo_id     phenotype_name             association_weight
#>   <chr>       <chr>     <chr>      <chr>                                   <dbl>
#> 1 GNRH1       2796      HP:0000044 hypogonadotrophic hypogon…                  1
#> 2 GNRHR       2798      HP:0000044 hypogonadotrophic hypogon…                  1

1.2 DrugBank targets

Leuprolide and calcitriol come from a saved DrugBank sample. Bivalirudin is parsed from a DrugBank XML record.

two_drugs <- readRDS(system.file("two_drugs.RDS", package = "dbparser"))

bivalirudin <- parseDrugBank(
  db_path            = system.file("extdata",
                                   "drugbank_record_small_molecule.xml",
                                   package = "dbparser"),
  drug_options       = NULL,
  parse_salts        = FALSE,
  parse_products     = FALSE,
  references_options = NULL,
  cett_options       = "targets")

2. Link drug targets to phenotypes

merge_drugbank_hpo() maps each DrugBank target to its gene and adds drugbank_id and drug_name to the HPO associations. We merge each DrugBank object and stack the results.

merged <- lapply(list(two_drugs, bivalirudin), merge_drugbank_hpo,
                 hpo_db = hpo_db)

# drug -> target -> gene bridge, including targets without HPO data
gene_bridge <- bind_rows(lapply(merged, function(m) {
  m$integrated_data$DrugBank_GeneSymbol_Mapping
}))

# HPO associations of the drug target genes
target_phenotypes <- bind_rows(lapply(merged, function(m) {
  m$integrated_data$gene_phenotype_enriched
})) %>%
  filter(!is.na(drugbank_id)) %>%
  distinct(drug_name, gene_symbol, hpo_id, phenotype_name)

gene_bridge %>%
  select(drug_name, target_id, polypeptide_name, gene_name) %>%
  left_join(count(target_phenotypes, gene_symbol, name = "hpo_terms"),
            by = c("gene_name" = "gene_symbol"))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   drug_name   target_id polypeptide_name                     gene_name hpo_terms
#>   <chr>       <chr>     <chr>                                <chr>         <int>
#> 1 Leuprolide  BE0000203 Gonadotropin-releasing hormone rece… GNRHR            30
#> 2 Leuprolide  BE0010526 Progonadoliberin-1                   GNRH1            24
#> 3 Calcitriol  BE0000779 Vitamin D3 receptor                  VDR             183
#> 4 Calcitriol  BE0008987 Homeobox protein Hox-A10             HOXA10           NA
#> 5 Bivalirudin BE0000048 Prothrombin                          F2               71

Four of the five targets have HPO annotations. HOXA10, a target that DrugBank lists for calcitriol with an unknown role (known_action = "unknown"), has none. Missing phenotypes are a coverage gap, not evidence that the target is safe to modulate.

GNRH1 encodes the GnRH precursor, the natural ligand of the GnRH receptor. Leuprolide is a GnRH analogue, so GNRH1 and GNRHR describe the same signalling axis.

3. Keep the informative phenotypes

Harmonizome propagates every annotation up the ontology. A gene annotated with epistaxis is also annotated with abnormality of the nose, phenotypic abnormality and the root term all. These grouping terms, the inheritance and onset terms, and the clinical modifiers say nothing about the gene, so we drop them.

is_uninformative <- function(hpo_id, phenotype_name) {
  hpo_id %in% c("HP:0000001", "HP:0000118") |
    grepl("inheritance|onset|clinical modifier|variability|expressivity",
          phenotype_name) |
    grepl("^(functional )?abnormal(ity)? ", phenotype_name) |
    grepl(" abnormality$|anomaly", phenotype_name)
}

specific_phenotypes <- target_phenotypes %>%
  filter(!is_uninformative(hpo_id, phenotype_name))

count(target_phenotypes, drug_name, gene_symbol, name = "all_terms") %>%
  left_join(count(specific_phenotypes, drug_name, gene_symbol,
                  name = "specific_terms"),
            by = c("drug_name", "gene_symbol"))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   drug_name   gene_symbol all_terms specific_terms
#>   <chr>       <chr>           <int>          <int>
#> 1 Bivalirudin F2                 71             21
#> 2 Calcitriol  VDR               183             70
#> 3 Leuprolide  GNRH1              24              6
#> 4 Leuprolide  GNRHR              30             11

This name-based filter is a quick heuristic. For a full analysis, filter on the ontology structure instead, e.g. by keeping only the most specific terms with the ontologyIndex package and the HPO .obo file.

4. Group phenotypes into clinical domains

To compare targets, we assign each phenotype to a clinical domain with keyword rules. The rules are applied in order, and the first match wins.

domain_rules <- c(
  "Bleeding & coagulation"   = "hemorrhag|bleed|epistaxis|menorrhagia|bruising|prothrombin|thromboplastin",
  "Thrombosis"               = "thrombo(sis|phlebitis)|embolism",
  "Reproductive & gonadal"   = "gonad|puberty|genital|test[ei]|amenorrh|menstrua|androgen",
  "Calcium & mineral"        = "calc|phosphat|parathyroid|vitamin|alkaline|nephrolith",
  "Skeletal & dental"        = "bone|skelet|rickets|bowing|bossing|fractur|osteo|epiphys|metaphys|fontanel|sutur|rib|costochondral|genu|scoliosis|teeth|dental|enamel|occiput|cephaly|wrist|ankle|trabecul|cortex|stature",
  "Neuromuscular & growth"   = "seizure|hypotonia|motor|gait|muscle|walking|standing|irritab|neurodevelop|anosmia|growth|thrive|body weight"
)

assign_domain <- function(phenotype_name) {
  domain <- rep("Other", length(phenotype_name))
  for (rule in rev(names(domain_rules))) {
    domain[grepl(domain_rules[[rule]], phenotype_name)] <- rule
  }
  domain
}

specific_phenotypes <- specific_phenotypes %>%
  mutate(domain = assign_domain(phenotype_name),
         drug_target = paste0(drug_name, " (", gene_symbol, ")"))

domain_counts <- specific_phenotypes %>%
  count(drug_target, domain)

domain_counts
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3
#>    drug_target        domain                     n
#>    <chr>              <chr>                  <int>
#>  1 Bivalirudin (F2)   Bleeding & coagulation    12
#>  2 Bivalirudin (F2)   Other                      1
#>  3 Bivalirudin (F2)   Reproductive & gonadal     2
#>  4 Bivalirudin (F2)   Thrombosis                 6
#>  5 Calcitriol (VDR)   Calcium & mineral         10
#>  6 Calcitriol (VDR)   Neuromuscular & growth    15
#>  7 Calcitriol (VDR)   Other                      5
#>  8 Calcitriol (VDR)   Skeletal & dental         40
#>  9 Leuprolide (GNRH1) Neuromuscular & growth     2
#> 10 Leuprolide (GNRH1) Reproductive & gonadal     4
#> 11 Leuprolide (GNRHR) Reproductive & gonadal    11

The plot below shows each target’s phenotype profile.

domain_levels <- c(names(domain_rules), "Other")

tidy_to_matrix <- function(counts) {
  targets <- sort(unique(counts$drug_target))
  m <- matrix(0, nrow = length(domain_levels), ncol = length(targets),
              dimnames = list(domain_levels, targets))
  m[cbind(counts$domain, counts$drug_target)] <- counts$n
  as.data.frame(m)
}

canvasXpress(
  data             = tidy_to_matrix(domain_counts),
  graphType        = "Stacked",
  graphOrientation = "horizontal",
  title            = "Mendelian phenotypes of drug target genes",
  subtitle         = "Specific HPO terms per target, by clinical domain",
  xAxisTitle       = "Number of HPO terms",
  colorScheme      = "Tableau",
  legendPosition   = "right",
  showSampleNames  = TRUE
)

Each target has a distinct profile: F2 is dominated by bleeding and thrombosis, the GnRH axis genes by reproductive phenotypes, and VDR by skeletal and mineral phenotypes.

5. Interpret the phenotypes using the direction of drug action

HPO tells us what happens when a gene is altered, mostly by loss of function. It does not tell us whether a drug mimics or opposes that change. That depends on the drug’s action on the target.

For bivalirudin, the action comes from the parsed DrugBank record. Each CETT action row carries its drugbank_id, so we can read the action for this drug alone:

bivalirudin$cett$targets$actions %>%
  left_join(select(bivalirudin$cett$targets$general_information,
                   target_id, drugbank_id, target_name = name),
            by = c("target_id", "drugbank_id"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   action    target_id drugbank_id target_name
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <chr>       <chr>      
#> 1 inhibitor BE0000048 DB00006     Prothrombin

The two_drugs sample was saved before CETT actions carried a drugbank_id, so its actions table cannot be attributed to a single drug. For leuprolide and calcitriol we write down the mode of action from their DrugBank entries and their known pharmacology:

drug_direction <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug_name,    ~gene_symbol, ~action,     ~net_effect_on_target,
  "Bivalirudin", "F2",         "inhibitor", "loss of function",
  "Leuprolide",  "GNRHR",      "agonist",   "loss of function (desensitisation)",
  "Leuprolide",  "GNRH1",      "analogue",  "loss of function (desensitisation)",
  "Calcitriol",  "VDR",        "agonist",   "gain of function"
)
drug_direction
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   drug_name   gene_symbol action    net_effect_on_target              
#>   <chr>       <chr>       <chr>     <chr>                             
#> 1 Bivalirudin F2          inhibitor loss of function                  
#> 2 Leuprolide  GNRHR       agonist   loss of function (desensitisation)
#> 3 Leuprolide  GNRH1       analogue  loss of function (desensitisation)
#> 4 Calcitriol  VDR         agonist   gain of function

Leuprolide is a receptor agonist, but continuous exposure desensitises the GnRH receptor and shuts down the pituitary–gonadal axis. Its net effect is therefore similar to losing the receptor.

Now we look at the domains that best represent each target:

key_domains <- c("Bleeding & coagulation", "Thrombosis",
                 "Reproductive & gonadal", "Calcium & mineral")

specific_phenotypes %>%
  filter(domain %in% key_domains) %>%
  group_by(drug_target, domain) %>%
  summarise(n_terms  = n(),
            examples = paste(head(sort(phenotype_name), 5), collapse = "; "),
            .groups  = "drop") %>%
  arrange(drug_target, desc(n_terms)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
drug_target domain n_terms examples
Bivalirudin (F2) Bleeding & coagulation 12 bruising susceptibility; epistaxis; gastrointestinal hemorrhage; gingival bleeding; internal hemorrhage
Bivalirudin (F2) Thrombosis 6 cerebral venous thrombosis; deep venous thrombosis; pulmonary embolism; recurrent thrombophlebitis; thrombophlebitis
Bivalirudin (F2) Reproductive & gonadal 2 menstrual irregularities; puberty and gonadal disorders
Calcitriol (VDR) Calcium & mineral 10 elevated alkaline phosphatase; elevated circulating parathyroid hormone (pth) level; hyperparathyroidism; hypocalcemia; hypocalcemic seizures
Leuprolide (GNRH1) Reproductive & gonadal 4 delayed puberty; hypogonadism; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism; puberty and gonadal disorders
Leuprolide (GNRHR) Reproductive & gonadal 11 amenorrhea; androgen insufficiency; aplasia/hypoplasia of the testes; decreased testicular size; external genital hypoplasia

The two reproductive terms for F2 (menstrual irregularities and puberty and gonadal disorders) are most likely ancestors of menorrhagia that the propagation added. They reflect bleeding, not a separate reproductive effect.

Bivalirudin and F2: phenotypes predict the main adverse effect

Bivalirudin inhibits thrombin, so it mimics loss of F2 function. Prothrombin deficiency causes bleeding: epistaxis, gingival and gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times. Bleeding is the main adverse effect of bivalirudin, and a prolonged clotting time is how its effect is monitored. The thrombosis terms come from the gain-of-function variant (prothrombin G20210A). They describe the state that the drug is given to oppose, not a predicted adverse effect.

Leuprolide and the GnRH axis: phenotypes predict the therapeutic effect

Loss of GNRHR or GNRH1 causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, androgen insufficiency, amenorrhoea and delayed puberty. Leuprolide causes the same state in patients on purpose. It is the basis of androgen deprivation therapy in prostate cancer and of its use in endometriosis and central precocious puberty. It also explains the drug’s hypogonadal adverse effects. GNRH1 alone also adds anosmia. Anosmia belongs to the Kallmann form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, where GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons fail to develop. The term is probably attached to GNRH1 through a disease entry that covers hypogonadism “with or without anosmia”. It reflects development, not GnRH signalling, so it is not expected from leuprolide. Checks like this are part of reading gene-level annotations.

Calcitriol and VDR: the direction is reversed

Loss of VDR causes hereditary vitamin D–resistant rickets: rickets, hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism and alopecia. Calcitriol activates the receptor, so these phenotypes do not predict its adverse effects. They describe the deficiency state that calcitriol treats. The main adverse effects of calcitriol, hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria, come from too much receptor activity, and the loss-of-function annotations do not contain them.

6. Compare the phenotype profiles

The bar chart shows how many terms each target has; VDR dominates because vitamin D-resistant rickets is a multi-system disease that is described in detail. To compare the composition of the profiles, we convert the counts to the share of each target’s specific terms that fall in each domain.

domain_share <- domain_counts %>%
  group_by(drug_target) %>%
  mutate(n = round(100 * n / sum(n))) %>%
  ungroup()

canvasXpress(
  data                      = as.data.frame(t(tidy_to_matrix(domain_share))),
  graphType                 = "Heatmap",
  title                     = "Phenotype profile of each drug target",
  subtitle                  = "Share of specific HPO terms (%)",
  colorSpectrum             = c("white", "#08519c"),
  showHeatmapIndicator      = TRUE,
  heatmapIndicatorPosition  = "right",
  heatmapIndicatorHistogram = FALSE,
  samplesClustered          = FALSE,
  variablesClustered        = FALSE,
  showSampleNames           = TRUE,
  showVariableNames         = TRUE
)

The profiles hardly overlap. Each target points to one organ system, and that system matches the drug’s known pharmacology: haemostasis for bivalirudin, the reproductive axis for leuprolide, and bone and mineral metabolism for calcitriol. The two GnRH axis genes have similar profiles, as expected for a ligand and its receptor.

Conclusion

Linking DrugBank targets to HPO phenotypes takes three calls: parseHPO(), parseDrugBank() and merge_drugbank_hpo(). In this example the Mendelian phenotypes of the target genes agreed with known pharmacology once the direction of drug action was taken into account:

  1. For an inhibitor (bivalirudin), the loss-of-function phenotypes predict the main adverse effect, bleeding.
  2. For a drug whose net effect is suppression (leuprolide), they predict the therapeutic effect, hypogonadism.
  3. For an agonist (calcitriol), they describe the disease being treated, and the adverse effects lie in the opposite direction.

Before using these annotations to anticipate effects for a new compound, check the direction of action. Also treat genes without annotations (HOXA10 here) as unknown, not as safe.
